Case Study: A Cultural-Fest Seating Grid

Read the passage carefully, then answer the 5 MCQs in the test below.

A school cultural-fest committee arranges chairs in a hall as a rectangular grid and records the layout as a matrix, one entry for each chair. For the prize ceremony they must seat exactly 36 guests in a perfect rectangle with no empty chair, so the head usher lists every possible number of rows and columns. For the choir they fix a 3×4 block and number its chairs by the rule a_(ij)=4(i-1)+j, read row by row. A last-minute change forces two overlapping seat counts to agree: the committee writes a single matrix equation whose corresponding entries give the unknown counts of boys and girls. Throughout, the usher keeps repeating one rule of thumb — first fix the order of a layout, because the order alone decides whether two seating charts can even be compared, before you ever look at the individual chairs.

questions.q: The number of distinct rectangular layouts (orders m× n) that seat exactly 36 guests is
questions.explanation: A rectangle with 36 chairs has an order m× n for each factor pair of 36: 1×36,\ 2×18,\ 3×12,\ 4×9,\ 6×6,\ 9×4,\ 12×3,\ 18×2,\ 36×1 — nine orders. (b).

questions.q: In the choir block with a_(ij)=4(i-1)+j, the chair number a₃₂ is

questions.explanation: Equating entries: x+y=10 and x-y=4. Adding gives 2x=14, so x=7 (and y=3). (a).

questions.q: Among the layouts seating 36 guests, the one that is a square matrix has order
questions.explanation: A square matrix needs equal rows and columns; among the factor pairs of 36 only 6×6 qualifies. (d).

questions.q: Two seating charts A and B describe the very same arrangement (A=B) exactly when
options: they seat the same number of guests
they have the same order and equal corresponding entries
they have the same total of entries
one is the transpose of the other
questions.explanation: By the definition of equality, A=B requires the same order and a_(ij)=b_(ij) for every i,j. (b).
